sections.h: Why New Dryers Come Without a Cord

blocks.p: Buy an electric dryer in the United States and there is a good chance it comes without a power cord. That surprises people, but it is deliberate. American homes have two different 30-amp dryer outlets in common use, the older three-prong NEMA 10-30 and the newer four-prong NEMA 14-30, and the dryer manufacturer cannot know which one you have. So the dryer ships with a terminal block and a bonding strap, and you or the installer add the cord that matches your wall.

That makes choosing the best dryer cord a simple job, and a surprisingly important one. A cord that matches your outlet, carries a listing mark, reaches without strain, and is installed with the bonding strap set the way the dryer manual says is a safe, permanent connection. A cord that does not match, or an adapter bolted on to force a mismatch, is how dryer installs go wrong. The cord is cheap; getting it right is what matters.

The good news is that the cords themselves are commodities. A four-wire 30-amp cord from one listed brand is electrically the same as another, and the real choices are type and length. The products below were chosen because they are widely available under clear names, come in both three- and four-wire versions, and are what you will find at home centers and appliance stores.

This guide is about electric dryers. Gas dryers run on a standard 120-volt cord and plug into an ordinary household outlet for the drum motor, controls and igniter, so they never need a 30-amp dryer cord. If you are in a laundry room thinking about electrical upgrades more broadly, our pillar guide to the [best whole-house surge protectors](/best-whole-house-surge-protector/) covers protection for the dryer, washer and every other appliance on the panel.

A three prong dryer outlet is a NEMA 10-30 receptacle. It has two angled slots for the two hot conductors and one L-shaped slot for the neutral, and no separate ground. A four-prong outlet is a NEMA 14-30: two straight vertical slots for the hots, an L-shaped neutral, and a round or U-shaped ground. Both are 30 amp dryer outlet designs on a 120/240-volt circuit, and both are fed by a double-pole 30-amp breaker; the difference is whether the ground has its own wire.

That difference matters because of how the dryer's metal cabinet is grounded. In a four-wire setup the cabinet is connected to a dedicated equipment ground, and the neutral carries only the dryer's 120-volt current for the timer, lights and motor. In a three-wire setup, the cabinet is bonded to the neutral, so the neutral does double duty. If that neutral ever loosens or breaks, the dryer cabinet can become energized, which is the reason the code moved away from it.

The 1996 edition of the National Electrical Code began requiring four-wire circuits for new dryer and range installations. States and cities adopt code editions on their own schedules, so the change reached different areas at different times, but most homes wired from the late 1990s on have four-prong outlets. Existing three-wire circuits were allowed to remain in service, which is why millions of older homes still have the three-prong type and why three-wire cords are still sold.

There is no prize for guessing which one you have. Look at the outlet, count the slots, and compare the shapes to the descriptions above. If the outlet looks damaged, scorched or loose, stop there and call an electrician, because no new cord fixes a failing receptacle. If you need to turn off the circuit to inspect it, a [circuit breaker finder](/best-circuit-breaker-finder/) will confirm which double-pole breaker feeds the laundry before you open anything.

blocks.p: Notice what is not on the list: adapters. There is no 4 prong to 3 prong dryer adapter, and no dryer 3 prong to 4 prong converter, among our picks, and that is not an oversight. The correct way to connect a dryer to a given outlet is a cord that matches it. The section after the picks explains why, and what to do if your dryer and your outlet disagree.

sections.h: Dryer Cord Converters and Adapters: Why the Answer Is a New Cord

blocks.p: The most common reason people go looking for a dryer cord converter is a move. The old house had a three-prong outlet, the new one has four, and the dryer's existing three-wire cord does not fit. Or the reverse. The quick search turns up short adapter pigtails that plug into one outlet type and accept the other plug. They are sold, they look official, and they are the wrong answer.

A 4 prong to 3 prong dryer adapter, or its reverse, leaves the dryer's grounding arrangement mismatched with the wiring. Plug a three-wire cord, with the dryer's bonding strap in place, into a four-wire outlet through an adapter, and the cabinet ground and the neutral are tied together at the dryer while the house wiring expects them to be separate. Going the other way, a four-wire dryer without its strap connected to a three-wire outlet can leave the cabinet with no ground at all. Neither is something an inspector would accept, and neither is something the dryer manual permits.

Adapters also add two more contact points on a circuit that carries close to 30 amps for an hour or more at a time. Loose or poor contacts on high-current circuits heat up, and heat is how dryer connections fail. A cord costs about the same as an adapter, often less, and replacing it takes about the same time as a careful adapter install. There is simply no good reason to use one.

So the real dryer 3 prong to 4 prong converter is a four-wire cord, installed with the bonding strap removed or relocated per the manual, and the real 4 to 3 converter is a three-wire cord with the strap installed. Keep the old cord in a labeled bag taped to the back of the dryer if you move often; next time, you will have both. The one thing you should never do is change the wall outlet to match the cord yourself, which section six covers.
THE RULE
Match the cord to the outlet. Never adapt the outlet to the cord.

Buy a cord with the same plug as your receptacle, and set the dryer's bonding strap the way its manual says for that cord type. Adapters between three- and four-prong dryer plugs are not a substitute.

sections.h: The Bonding Strap: The Step Most People Get Wrong

blocks.p: Behind the access cover on the back of an electric dryer is a terminal block with three screws, plus a separate green ground screw on the cabinet. On most models a small metal strap or a green-and-yellow wire connects the center neutral terminal to the cabinet. That is the bonding strap, and its position is the difference between a correct and an incorrect installation.

With a three-wire cord, the strap stays in place. The two hot conductors go to the outer terminals, the neutral goes to the center terminal, and the strap bonds the neutral to the cabinet so the cabinet is grounded through the neutral. With a four-wire cord, the hots and neutral go to the same three terminals, the green ground conductor goes to the cabinet ground screw, and the bonding strap is removed or moved to the ground screw, depending on the manufacturer. The dryer manual and the diagram on the back of the dryer say exactly which.

Getting this backward is common. A four-wire cord installed with the strap still in place ties the neutral to the cabinet and to the ground conductor, which defeats the point of having a separate ground. A three-wire cord installed without the strap leaves the cabinet ungrounded. Neither error stops the dryer from working, which is exactly why they go unnoticed. Take a photo of the terminal block before you start, and follow the manual, not memory or a video for a different brand.

Before touching the terminal block, unplug the dryer, not just switch it off. If the old cord is hardwired or you have any doubt, turn off the double-pole breaker and confirm the circuit is dead with a tester. Install the strain relief where the cord enters the cabinet so the cord cannot be pulled against the terminals, tighten the terminal screws firmly, and replace the cover. If any part of this is unfamiliar, an appliance installer or electrician can do it in a few minutes.

sections.h: Changing the Receptacle Is an Electrician Job

blocks.p: Sometimes the outlet itself is the problem. It may be cracked, scorched, worn so the plug falls out, or simply the older three-prong type in a house you want to bring up to date. All of those are good reasons to change it, and all of them are jobs for a licensed electrician, often with a permit depending on where you live.

Converting a three-prong outlet to four-prong is not a matter of swapping the receptacle. A NEMA 14-30 needs a separate equipment ground conductor running back to the panel, and most three-wire dryer circuits do not have one. The electrician will either run a new four-wire circuit or add a ground conductor by a method the code permits. Simply installing a four-prong receptacle on a three-wire cable, with the ground slot tied to the neutral, creates exactly the hidden hazard the code change was meant to eliminate.

Going the other way, replacing a four-prong outlet with a three-prong one so an old cord fits, is not allowed and makes no sense: you would be downgrading a safer circuit to match a cheap part. Buy the four-wire cord instead. Likewise, never change the breaker size to suit an appliance. A 30-amp dryer circuit should have a 30-amp double-pole breaker and wire sized for it, typically 10 AWG copper.

While the electrician is at the panel, it is a good moment to add a [whole-house surge protector](/best-whole-house-surge-protector/), since modern dryers have electronic control boards that are as vulnerable to surges as any other appliance. If you also run a generator, ask about a proper inlet and switch; our guide to the [best generator transfer switch](/best-generator-transfer-switch/) explains why a dryer outlet must never be used to feed generator power into the house.

Dryer cords are commonly sold in lengths from about four to ten feet. Measure from the outlet to the terminal block on the back of the dryer, add enough slack for the dryer to be pulled out for vent cleaning, and buy the next length up. Four feet works when the outlet is directly behind the dryer; five or six feet suits most other layouts. A ten-foot cord is for unusual setups and leaves a lot to coil.

Too short is worse than too long. A cord stretched tight puts strain on the plug blades and the terminal block, and those are the places where heat-related failures start. Too long is mostly a tidiness problem, but avoid piling coils behind the dryer where lint collects, and never run the cord under the dryer feet or pinch it against the wall when you push the machine back.

Never use an extension cord for a dryer. Ordinary extension cords are not rated for a 30-amp, 240-volt appliance, and even heavy-duty ones are not made for the plug types involved. If no standard cord length reaches, the outlet is in the wrong place and an electrician should move it, or the dryer should be positioned closer.

Thirty-amp dryer cords generally use 10-gauge conductors, which is what the 30-amp rating calls for; check the cord jacket or listing if in doubt. Every cord needs a strain relief, a clamp that fastens the cord to the dryer's cabinet where it enters, so a tug on the cord does not reach the terminals. Some cords include one and some do not. Reusing the old strain relief is fine if it fits the new cord's diameter and is undamaged.

sections.h: Manufactured Homes, Rentals and Stackable Units

blocks.p: Some installations never allowed three-wire dryer connections. Dryer manufacturers typically state in their installation instructions that a four-wire connection is required in manufactured or mobile homes, in new construction, and anywhere local codes prohibit grounding the cabinet through the neutral. If any of those apply to you, the three-wire cords on this list are not an option, and a three-prong outlet in that setting needs an electrician's attention.

Renters are in a tighter spot. You can and should buy the cord that matches the outlet in your unit, and swapping a dryer's cord is normally within a tenant's purview since the dryer is yours. Changing the receptacle or the circuit is not; that is the landlord's job and an electrician's work. If the outlet is damaged, report it in writing rather than working around it. Keep both cord types if you move between rentals often.

Stacked washer-dryer units and compact 240-volt dryers usually follow the same rules, but some compact European-style units use a different plug or are designed for a different circuit entirely. Read the installation instructions before buying anything. If your dryer is a 120-volt compact model, it plugs into an ordinary outlet and none of these cords apply; our guide to the [best portable dryer](/best-portable-dryer/) covers those machines.

If you are setting up a new laundry space entirely, including a [portable washer](/best-portable-washer/) or relocating appliances, plan the electrical first. A new dryer circuit will be four-wire by code, so buy a four-wire cord and let the electrician set the outlet location so a standard length reaches without strain.

If your outlet has four prongs, buy a four-wire NEMA 14-30 cord. The Certified Appliance Accessories four-wire cord is the default choice because it is widely stocked in several lengths. Choose the Whirlpool PT220 if you prefer a brand-name cord and the outlet is close behind the dryer, the Smart Choice four-wire six-foot cord if the outlet is off to one side, or the Eastman four-wire if that is what your store has.

If your outlet has three prongs and the circuit is an existing, grandfathered one, buy a three-wire NEMA 10-30 cord. The Certified Appliance Accessories three-wire cord is the default, and the Smart Choice three-wire six-foot cord is the longer option. Make sure the bonding strap is installed per the dryer manual, and consider an electrician's upgrade to four-wire next time the laundry room is opened up.

Do not buy an adapter, do not swap the wall outlet yourself, and do not use an extension cord. If the outlet is damaged, the plug fits loosely, or you see scorch marks on the plug or terminal block, stop and call a licensed electrician before running the dryer again. Those are signs of a connection that is overheating, and a new cord is only part of the fix.

Finally, a dryer is one appliance on a panel full of electronics. A [whole-house surge protector](/best-whole-house-surge-protector/) covers its control board along with everything else, and if you are curious how much your dryer actually uses, the best home energy monitors will show you load by circuit. It is often the biggest single electric load in the house after heating and cooling.

mistakes: Adapters leave the dryer's grounding arrangement mismatched with the house wiring and add extra high-current contact points that can overheat. They are not what dryer manufacturers or inspectors accept. The correct fix is a cord that matches the outlet, installed with the bonding strap set as the dryer's manual describes for that cord type.
Leaving the bonding strap in with a 4-wire cord

With a four-wire cord, the neutral and ground must stay separate at the dryer, so the bonding strap is removed or relocated per the manual. Leaving it in place bonds the neutral to the cabinet and defeats the separate ground. The dryer will still run, which is why this mistake so often goes unnoticed.
Swapping a 3-prong outlet for a 4-prong one

A four-prong receptacle needs a real equipment ground wire back to the panel, which most three-wire dryer circuits lack. Installing one with the ground tied to the neutral hides the hazard instead of fixing it. Converting the circuit is a job for a licensed electrician, often with a permit.
Buying a range cord for a dryer

Range cords are rated 40 or 50 amps and have different plugs that will not fit a 30-amp dryer outlet. They look similar on the shelf, so check the packaging for 30 amps and the NEMA 10-30 or 14-30 plug type that matches your receptacle before you leave the store.
Choosing a cord that is too short

A cord stretched tight strains the plug blades and the terminal block, which is where heat-related failures begin. Measure from the outlet to the dryer's terminal block, allow slack for pulling the dryer out to clean the vent, and buy the next standard length up. Never add an extension cord.
bottomLine: The best dryer cord is the one that matches your outlet: a four-wire NEMA 14-30 cord for four-prong outlets, a three-wire NEMA 10-30 cord for existing three-prong outlets. Install it with the bonding strap set exactly as your dryer's manual says, with a strain relief, and long enough to reach without tension. Skip adapters, never use an extension cord, and leave receptacle changes and circuit upgrades to a licensed electrician.

faqs.q: What is the best dryer cord?
faqs.a: The best dryer cord is a listed 30-amp cord whose plug matches your outlet and whose length reaches without strain. For four-prong NEMA 14-30 outlets, a four-wire cord such as the Certified Appliance Accessories four-wire or Whirlpool PT220 is the right choice. For existing three-prong NEMA 10-30 outlets, a three-wire cord such as the Certified Appliance Accessories three-wire is correct. Brand matters far less than type and length.

faqs.q: Can I use a 4 prong to 3 prong dryer adapter?
faqs.a: It is not recommended. Adapters between three- and four-prong dryer plugs leave the dryer's grounding mismatched with the wiring and add extra connections on a high-current circuit. Dryer manufacturers' instructions call for a cord that matches the outlet, with the bonding strap set for that cord type. A new cord costs about the same as an adapter and is the safe, accepted fix.

faqs.q: How do I convert my dryer from 3 prong to 4 prong?
faqs.a: If the wall outlet is already four-prong, replace the dryer's three-wire cord with a four-wire 14-30 cord and remove or relocate the bonding strap as the dryer manual describes. If the wall outlet is three-prong and you want four-prong, that requires adding a ground conductor or a new circuit, which is a job for a licensed electrician, usually with a permit.

faqs.q: Are three prong dryer outlets still legal?
faqs.a: Existing three-prong dryer outlets are generally allowed to remain in service under the National Electrical Code, which began requiring four-wire circuits for new installations in its 1996 edition. New circuits must be four-wire. Manufacturers also say three-wire connections are not permitted in manufactured homes or where local codes prohibit them, so check your situation if you are unsure.

faqs.q: What size breaker and wire does a 30 amp dryer outlet need?
faqs.a: A standard electric dryer circuit uses a 30-amp double-pole breaker and copper conductors typically sized at 10 AWG, feeding either a NEMA 10-30 or NEMA 14-30 receptacle. Always check your dryer's nameplate and installation instructions. Never install a larger breaker to stop nuisance tripping; a tripping breaker is a symptom for an electrician to diagnose.

faqs.q: Is a Smart Choice dryer cord any good?
faqs.a: Smart Choice is an appliance accessory line associated with Frigidaire and sold through many retailers, and its three- and four-wire dryer cords are rated for 30-amp dryer circuits like other listed cords. There is nothing special about them electrically compared with other listed brands. Choose the version that matches your outlet and the length you need, and confirm whether a strain relief is included.

faqs.q: Can I install a dryer cord myself?
faqs.a: Many homeowners replace a dryer cord themselves, since it attaches to the dryer's terminal block rather than the house wiring. Unplug the dryer first, follow the dryer manual's wiring diagram for your cord type, set the bonding strap correctly and install a strain relief. If anything is unclear, or the outlet looks damaged, have an appliance installer or licensed electrician handle it.
